newsitem.title: USA: Watergate wars still rage on 25 years later.
newsitem.headline: Watergate wars still rage on 25 years later.

text.p: Tempers are still flaring among some of the central figures in the Watergate political scandal 25 years later.

Older and grayer but still sharp of mind on the intricate details of Watergate, some of the people involved in the events that brought down President Richard Nixon spent two days haggling about it this week to mark the scandal's 25th anniversary.

It was on June 17, 1972 that a bungled break-in of the Democratic National Committee headquarters at the Watergate Hotel led to a series of cataclysmic revelations that eventually forced Nixon's resignation on Aug. 8, 1974. He died three years ago.

John Dean, the boyish 33-year-old White House counsel whose turncoat testimony that Nixon was involved in the Watergate coverup was central to the case, is now a silver-haired, 58-year-old California investment banker.

On Thursday night he appeared at a Watergate retrospective with Sam Dash, who was the aggressive chief counsel of the Senate Select Committee on Watergate, and Leonard Garment, who was a special consultant and later a counsel to Nixon. Dash is now a Georgetown University professor and Garment works at a Washington law firm.

Battle lines were drawn early and often between Dash, who considered Nixon guilty of "pervasive criminality," and Garment, who said Nixon was "a beleaguered man who did a lot of good things" for the country.
Garment scoffed when Dean defended himself for trying to get immunity from prosecution before he would testify against the president. "Familiar criminal behaviour," he said.

Then Garment and Dash engaged in a shouting match when Dash recounted how it was feared that Dean's life could be in danger if the Nixon White House found out he was telling all he knew to the prosecution.
"That's outrageous!" said Garment, fidgeting in his seat.
"To repeat that publicly. The man is dead, for heaven's sake," Garment said.

He angrily threatened to leave the event, held at the Newseum, a museum of the news industry. A group of reporters, many from the Watergate era, applauded Garment when he said, "I'm on the verge of just leaving."
But he hung around, only to be scolded by Dash.

"You have ignored the facts, Len, all through our discussion, and raised every kind of a smokescreen to avoid the historical importance of Watergate. Why you are doing this, I don't know. You were not involved, you came out clean. Why do you think you have to be a Watergate defender?" Dash said.
Garment's voice trailed off when he said "because there's nobody else here ..."

Nixon's ghost showed up at the retrospective, in the form of his voice recorded from the taping system that the president had installed to record his conversations for posterity but which ultimately proved him to be an active participant in the coverup.
His disembodied voice could be heard complaining that the press hounding of him about Watergate was a direct result of his much-criticised phased withdrawal of U.S. forces from the Vietnam War.
"If it hadn't been Watergate, it would've been something else," Nixon said.
